It distinguishes itself from simpler finite difference methods by employing a linear regression framework that produces nearly isotropic gradients with reduced fringing artifacts [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the Neumann gradient estimation method (which uses a linear regression framework and 26 neighboring voxels) 'produce[s] nearly isotropic gradients and less fringing artifacts than other methods.' It also notes that this method 'allows to filter the original voxels values with low additional computational costs' (interpreted as 'low additional cost' in the claim). While the evidence mentions 'considerably high computational costs' for the gradient estimation itself, the specific claim about the linear regression framework producing isotropic gradients with reduced artifacts and allowing filtering with low additional cost is directly supported by the text.
